title: Telling a story
topic: organizing a past narrative; time connectors; adverbs in -ment
why: This lesson closes the unit on memories by turning the two past tenses into real stories: setting, trigger, events and ending, linked with connectors like soudain, au bout d'un moment and le lendemain. You'll also learn adverbs in -ment and how to react when someone tells you a story.

{"lessons": ["

Setting the scene, moving the story

You know the two past tenses and how to choose between them. Now let's tell a real story, with a beginning, a twist and an ending. A good anecdote in French follows a simple shape:

StepTenseUseful words
1. The settingimparfaitC'était l'été, il faisait chaud, j'étais à…
2. The triggerpassé composéun jour, ce jour-là, soudain, tout à coup
3. What happened nextbothalors, pendant que, au bout d'un moment
4. The endingpassé composéfinalement, le lendemain
ConnectorEnglish
un jourone day
ce jour-làthat day
soudain, tout à coupsuddenly
alorsso, then
pendant quewhile
au bout d'un momentafter a while
finalementin the end, eventually
le lendemainthe next day
C'était l'été et j'étais en vacances à Nice. Un jour, je me promenais sur la plage. Soudain, j'ai vu un chien dans l'eau. Alors, j'ai appelé le chien et, au bout d'un moment, il est sorti de l'eau. Finalement, j'ai trouvé son maître. Le lendemain, le chien m'attendait devant l'hôtel !It was summer and I was on vacation in Nice. One day, I was walking on the beach. Suddenly, I saw a dog in the water. So I called the dog and, after a while, it came out of the water. In the end, I found its owner. The next day, the dog was waiting for me in front of the hotel!

Finalement means \"in the end\" or \"eventually\": this is the word English speakers want when they say éventuellement, which means \"possibly\". And le lendemain is \"the next day\" in a story; demain only works from today.

", "

Adverbs in -ment

French -ment is the English \"-ly\": lentement = slowly. To build it, take the feminine form of the adjective and add -ment.

Adjective (m. / f.)AdverbEnglish
lent / lentelentementslowly
heureux / heureuseheureusementfortunately, luckily
malheureux / malheureusemalheureusementunfortunately
doux / doucedoucementgently, quietly
sérieux / sérieusesérieusementseriously
final / finalefinalementin the end

Three special cases

  • When the masculine ends in a vowel, add -ment to the masculine: vrai → vraiment, poli → poliment, absolu → absolument.
  • -ant becomes -amment and -ent becomes -emment, both pronounced \"-amment\": constant → constamment, évident → évidemment.
  • Irregular: gentil → gentiment, bon → bien, mauvais → mal.

Where to put it

After the verb in the present and the imparfait: Il conduit lentement. In the passé composé, short common adverbs often go between the helper and the participle: J'ai vraiment aimé ce film. Adverbs that comment on the whole sentence go first, followed by a comma: Heureusement, le train était à l'heure.

Évidemment, il est arrivé en retard !Of course, he arrived late!
Malheureusement, le musée était fermé.Unfortunately, the museum was closed.

Remember the false friend actuellement: it looks like \"actually\", but it's built on actuel (current) and means \"currently\". Not every -ment adverb matches its English look-alike.

", "

Reacting to a story

A story is a conversation: the listener reacts, and the reactions push the storyteller to continue. Here are the most common ones:

ReactionMeaning
Ah bon ?Really? Is that so?
Et alors ?And then what?
Sans blague !No kidding!
C'est pas vrai !No way! You're kidding!
Oh là là !Oh dear! Wow!
Quelle chance !How lucky!
Heureusement !Thank goodness!

C'est pas vrai ! is the spoken form, without ne. In writing, it's Ce n'est pas vrai ! Et alors ? can also sound like \"So what?\" if you say it flatly: say it with curiosity, rising at the end.

—Hier, j'ai perdu mon portefeuille dans le métro. —Ah bon ? Et alors ? —Une dame l'a trouvé et elle l'a apporté à la police. —Quelle chance !—Yesterday I lost my wallet on the métro. —Really? And then? —A lady found it and took it to the police. —How lucky!

A story that ends well

Notice how the tenses alternate in an anecdote: the scene in the imparfait, then a chain of events in the passé composé, with adverbs to give your opinion.

Ce jour-là, il pleuvait et le train avançait lentement. Soudain, il s'est arrêté au milieu de la campagne. Au bout d'un moment, un contrôleur est passé. Heureusement, il était vraiment sympa, et finalement, nous sommes arrivés à Marseille avec seulement une heure de retard.That day, it was raining and the train was moving slowly. Suddenly, it stopped in the middle of the countryside. After a while, a conductor came by. Luckily, he was really nice, and in the end we arrived in Marseille only an hour late.

To start an anecdote among friends, French people often say Il m'est arrivé un truc incroyable ! (Something incredible happened to me!). Learn it as a fixed phrase.
